title: Random residuals, logarithmic fit
stem: A student fits a logarithmic model to a data set and graphs the residuals (actual output minus predicted output). The residual plot shows points scattered above and below zero with no visible pattern. This most strongly suggests that

correct.text: the logarithmic model is a reasonable fit for the data
correct.rationale: Residuals that are a mix of positive and negative values with no pattern indicate the model has captured the trend of the data; the leftover differences look like random variation.

wrong.text: every data point lies exactly on the logarithmic curve
wrong.rationale: If every point were exactly on the curve, every residual would be 0. The plot shows residuals above and below zero, so some are positive and some negative.
wrong.error_pattern: Equating a good fit with zero residuals

wrong.text: the logarithmic model is inappropriate because some residuals are not zero
wrong.rationale: Nonzero residuals are expected with real data. A poor model is signaled by a systematic pattern in the residuals, and this plot shows none.
wrong.error_pattern: Treating any nonzero residual as evidence of a bad model

wrong.text: the logarithmic model overestimates the output at every input
wrong.rationale: Overestimating at every input would make every residual (actual minus predicted) negative. The plot has points both above and below zero, so the model sometimes overestimates and sometimes underestimates.
wrong.error_pattern: Misreading residual signs

change_note: New model type (logarithmic), good-fit case rather than curvature case.

title: Sign pattern for a linear fit
stem: A linear model is fit to 12 data points, and the residuals (actual minus predicted) are plotted against x. The first four residuals are negative, the next four are positive, and the last four are negative. This most strongly suggests that

correct.text: the data have curvature that a linear model does not capture
correct.rationale: A residual sign pattern of negative, positive, negative across the whole range is structured. It shows the line sits above the data at both ends and below it in the middle, which indicates the data curve away from a straight line.

wrong.text: the data are exactly linear apart from a few outliers
wrong.rationale: Outliers would show up as a few isolated large residuals. Here the sign changes in a systematic run across the whole range (4 negative, 4 positive, 4 negative), which is a pattern, not isolated outliers.
wrong.error_pattern: Attributing a systematic pattern to outliers

wrong.text: the data are decreasing as x increases
wrong.rationale: Residuals compare the data to the fitted line; they do not show the direction of the data. Increasing data and decreasing data can both produce this negative-positive-negative pattern, so it gives no evidence about direction.
wrong.error_pattern: Confusing residual sign with trend direction

wrong.text: the slope of the linear model should be zero
wrong.rationale: The pattern points to curvature the line cannot follow. Nothing in a negative-positive-negative residual pattern implies the best line should be horizontal.
wrong.error_pattern: Reading the pattern as a slope problem

change_note: Linear model with explicit sign-run description instead of a U-shaped plot.

title: Comparing two residual plots
stem: Two models are fit to the same data set. The residual plot for Model A shows points scattered randomly above and below zero. The residual plot for Model B shows residuals that are positive for small inputs, negative for middle inputs, and positive for large inputs. Which statement is best supported?

correct.text: Model A is more appropriate because its residuals show no pattern
correct.rationale: Random scatter means Model A has captured the relationship. Model B's positive-negative-positive pattern means it leaves systematic structure unexplained.

wrong.text: Model B is more appropriate because its residuals follow a clear pattern
wrong.rationale: A clear residual pattern means the model is missing part of the relationship; it is evidence against the model, not for it.
wrong.error_pattern: Treating a residual pattern as a sign of a good fit

wrong.text: Neither model is appropriate because neither has all residuals equal to zero
wrong.rationale: Real data almost never give all-zero residuals. Appropriateness is judged by whether the residuals show a pattern, and Model A's do not.
wrong.error_pattern: Requiring zero residuals

wrong.text: The models cannot be compared without a correlation coefficient r
wrong.rationale: The residual plots themselves are direct evidence about whether each model form is appropriate. A high r can coexist with a clear residual pattern, so r is not needed to see that Model B leaves structure unexplained.
wrong.error_pattern: Relying on r instead of the residual pattern

change_note: Two-model comparison; asks which model is supported rather than interpreting a single plot.

title: Isotope half-life fraction
stem: A sample of an isotope has half-life 4 years. What fraction of the sample remains after 20 years?

correct.rationale: 20 years is 20/4 = 5 half-lives, so the fraction remaining is (1/2)^5 = 1/32.

wrong.rationale: Uses the number of half-lives, 20/4 = 5, as the denominator instead of raising 1/2 to the 5th power. The correct value is (1/2)^5 = 1/32, not 1/5.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the number of half-lives as the denominator

wrong.rationale: Multiplies the 5 half-lives by 2 to get the denominator, 5·2 = 10, instead of computing 2^5 = 32.
wrong.error_pattern: Multiplying rather than exponentiating

wrong.rationale: Squares the number of half-lives, 5² = 25, instead of raising 2 to that power, 2^5 = 32.
wrong.error_pattern: Swapping base and exponent

change_note: Different isotope, half-life, and elapsed time (5 half-lives).

title: Drug concentration percent
stem: A drug's concentration in the blood is cut in half every 6 hours. What percent of the original concentration remains after 24 hours?

correct.rationale: 24 hours is 24/6 = 4 half-lives, so the fraction is (1/2)^4 = 1/16 = 0.0625, or 6.25%.

wrong.rationale: Uses the number of half-lives, 4, as the denominator: 1/4 = 25%. The correct fraction is (1/2)^4 = 1/16.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the number of half-lives as the denominator

wrong.rationale: Counts only 24/6 − 1 = 3 half-lives, giving (1/2)^3 = 1/8 = 12.5%.
wrong.error_pattern: Off-by-one: one half-life too few

wrong.rationale: Counts five half-lives by listing the times 0, 6, 12, 18, 24 as five periods, giving (1/2)^5 = 1/32 = 3.125%.
wrong.error_pattern: Off-by-one: counting time points as intervals

change_note: Answer in percent, drug context, 4 half-lives.

title: Mass remaining of a sample
stem: A radioactive sample has mass 80 mg and loses half of its mass every 8 days. How many milligrams of the sample remain after 24 days?

correct.rationale: 24 days is 24/8 = 3 half-lives, so the mass is 80·(1/2)^3 = 80/8 = 10 mg.

wrong.rationale: Applies only two halvings: 80·(1/2)^2 = 20 mg. Three half-lives have passed.
wrong.error_pattern: Off-by-one: one half-life too few

wrong.rationale: Divides the starting mass by the number of half-lives: 80/3 ≈ 26.7 mg, instead of by 2^3 = 8.
wrong.error_pattern: Dividing by the number of half-lives

wrong.rationale: Subtracts the elapsed days from the starting mass: 80 − 24 = 56 mg, treating the decay as linear.
wrong.error_pattern: Treating exponential decay as linear

change_note: Starting amount given in mg, so answer is a mass, not a fraction.

title: Domain of a base-3 logarithm
stem: What is the domain of g(x) = log₃(9 − x²)?

correct.rationale: The argument must be positive: 9 − x² > 0, so x² < 9, which gives −3 < x < 3.

wrong.rationale: Solves 9 − x² < 0 (the wrong direction). For x = 4 the argument is 9 − 16 = −7, which is negative, so log₃ is undefined there.
wrong.error_pattern: Reversing the inequality

wrong.rationale: Includes the endpoints, but at x = 3 the argument is 9 − 9 = 0, and log₃(0) is undefined. The inequality must be strict.
wrong.error_pattern: Including endpoints where the argument is 0

wrong.rationale: Reduces x² < 9 to x < 3 and forgets the lower bound. For x = −5 the argument is 9 − 25 = −16, which is negative, so −5 is not in the domain.
wrong.error_pattern: Dropping the negative branch of x² < 9

change_note: Reflected quadratic argument (9 − x²) in base 3; answer is a bounded interval.

title: Domain of ln of a quadratic
stem: What is the domain of f(x) = ln(x² − x − 6)?

correct.rationale: x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2). The product is positive when both factors have the same sign, which gives x < −2 or x > 3.

wrong.rationale: This is where (x − 3)(x + 2) < 0. At x = 0 the argument is −6, which is negative, so ln is undefined there.
wrong.error_pattern: Choosing the region where the argument is negative

wrong.rationale: Factors as (x + 3)(x − 2), which expands to x² + x − 6, not x² − x − 6. At x = 2.5 the argument is 6.25 − 2.5 − 6 = −2.25, which is negative.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error when factoring

wrong.rationale: Includes the endpoints, but at x = 3 the argument is 9 − 3 − 6 = 0, and ln(0) is undefined.
wrong.error_pattern: Including endpoints where the argument is 0

change_note: Quadratic with linear term; factoring needed.

title: Domain of ln of a rational expression
stem: What is the domain of k(x) = ln((x + 1)/(x − 5))?

correct.rationale: The fraction (x + 1)/(x − 5) must be positive, so the numerator and denominator have the same sign: both positive gives x > 5, both negative gives x < −1.

wrong.rationale: This is where the fraction is negative. At x = 0 the argument is 1/(−5) = −1/5, so ln is undefined.
wrong.error_pattern: Choosing the region where the argument is negative

wrong.rationale: Requires only the numerator to be positive. At x = 0 the argument is −1/5, which is negative, so 0 is not in the domain.
wrong.error_pattern: Checking only the numerator

wrong.rationale: Excludes only the input that makes the argument 0 and the input that makes the denominator 0. The argument can also be negative, for example at x = 0 where it is −1/5.
wrong.error_pattern: Excluding only zeros of numerator and denominator

change_note: Rational argument inside ln; sign analysis of a quotient.

title: Gate rotation in radians
stem: A rotating gate turns through an angle of 210°. What is this angle in radians?

correct.rationale: Multiplying by π/180 gives 210π/180 = 7π/6.

wrong.rationale: Multiplies by π/90 instead of π/180: 210·π/90 = 7π/3, twice the correct measure.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong conversion factor (π/90)

wrong.rationale: Multiplies by π/360 instead of π/180: 210·π/360 = 7π/12, half the correct measure.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong conversion factor (π/360)

wrong.rationale: Inverts the ratio: uses 180/210 = 6/7 and attaches π to get 6π/7.
wrong.error_pattern: Inverting the conversion ratio

change_note: New angle (210°) in a rotation context.

title: Turntable angle in radians
stem: A turntable rotates through 135°. Which is the equivalent angle measure in radians?

correct.rationale: Multiplying by π/180 gives 135π/180 = 3π/4.

wrong.rationale: Multiplies by π/360 instead of π/180: 135·π/360 = 3π/8.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong conversion factor (π/360)

wrong.rationale: Inverts the ratio: 180/135 = 4/3, so 4π/3.
wrong.error_pattern: Inverting the conversion ratio

wrong.rationale: Multiplies by π but forgets to divide by 180, giving 135π.
wrong.error_pattern: Forgetting to divide by 180

change_note: 135° with a turntable context; different error set.

title: Negative angle to radians
stem: A clockwise rotation of 120° is represented by the angle −120°. What is −120° in radians?

correct.rationale: Multiplying by π/180 gives −120π/180 = −2π/3.

wrong.rationale: Converts the magnitude correctly but drops the negative sign, which indicates clockwise rotation.
wrong.error_pattern: Dropping the sign

wrong.rationale: Inverts the ratio: 180/120 = 3/2, giving −3π/2.
wrong.error_pattern: Inverting the conversion ratio

wrong.rationale: Multiplies by π/360 instead of π/180: −120·π/360 = −π/3.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong conversion factor (π/360)

change_note: Negative angle, clockwise context.

title: Tide model amplitude and midline
stem: The height of the tide in a harbor is modeled by a sinusoidal function with maximum 7.4 m, minimum 1.2 m, and period 12.4 hours. What are the amplitude and the midline of the model?

correct.rationale: Amplitude is half the range: (7.4 − 1.2)/2 = 3.1. The midline is the average of the extremes: (7.4 + 1.2)/2 = 4.3.

wrong.rationale: Uses the full range, 7.4 − 1.2 = 6.2, as the amplitude. Amplitude is half the range, 3.1.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the full range as amplitude

wrong.rationale: Gets the amplitude right, 3.1, but takes the maximum, 7.4, as the midline. The midline is the average of the maximum and minimum, 4.3.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the maximum as the midline

wrong.rationale: Interchanges the two quantities: the amplitude is 3.1 and the midline is y = 4.3.
wrong.error_pattern: Interchanging amplitude and midline

change_note: Decimal values in a tide context; period is a distractor not used.

title: Amplitude and midline from extremes
stem: A sinusoidal function f has a minimum value of −2 and a maximum value of 10. Which gives its amplitude and its midline?

correct.rationale: Amplitude is half the range: (10 − (−2))/2 = 6. The midline is the average: (10 + (−2))/2 = 4.

wrong.rationale: Uses the full range, 10 − (−2) = 12, as the amplitude. Amplitude is half of that, 6.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the full range as amplitude

wrong.rationale: Gets the amplitude right, but finds the midline as the sum 10 + (−2) = 8 without dividing by 2. The midline is 8/2 = 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Forgetting to divide the sum by 2

wrong.rationale: Interchanges the two quantities: the amplitude is 6 and the midline is y = 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Interchanging amplitude and midline

change_note: Negative minimum; no period given.

title: Amplitude and midline from two points
stem: A sinusoidal function has a highest point at (0.5, 9). The next lowest point to its right is (3.5, 1). Which gives the amplitude and the midline?

correct.rationale: Amplitude is half the vertical distance between the extremes: (9 − 1)/2 = 4. The midline is y = (9 + 1)/2 = 5.

wrong.rationale: Uses the full vertical distance, 9 − 1 = 8, as the amplitude. Amplitude is half of that, 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the full range as amplitude

wrong.rationale: Interchanges the two quantities: the amplitude is 4 and the midline is y = 5.
wrong.error_pattern: Interchanging amplitude and midline

wrong.rationale: Uses the horizontal distance between the points, 3.5 − 0.5 = 3, as the amplitude. Amplitude is measured vertically and equals 4.
wrong.error_pattern: Confusing horizontal distance with amplitude

change_note: Extremes given as coordinate points, requiring the y-values to be extracted.

title: Cosine equation on [0, 2π)
stem: On the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π, which gives all solutions of 2cos x = −√2?

correct.rationale: cos x = −√2/2. Cosine is negative in Quadrants II and III, where the reference angle π/4 gives x = π − π/4 = 3π/4 and x = π + π/4 = 5π/4.

wrong.rationale: These are the solutions of cos x = +√2/2. The negative sign on the right side was dropped.
wrong.error_pattern: Dropping the negative sign

wrong.rationale: These have cosine −√3/2, from using the reference angle π/6 instead of π/4. cos(5π/6) = −√3/2 ≈ −0.866, not −√2/2 ≈ −0.707.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong reference angle

wrong.rationale: Pairs Quadrant II with Quadrant IV, but cosine is positive in Quadrant IV: cos(7π/4) = +√2/2, not −√2/2.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong quadrant pairing

change_note: Cosine instead of sine; reference angle π/4.

title: Negative sine equation
stem: On the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π, which gives all solutions of 2sin x + 1 = 0?

correct.rationale: sin x = −1/2. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV, where the reference angle π/6 gives x = π + π/6 = 7π/6 and x = 2π − π/6 = 11π/6.

wrong.rationale: These are the solutions of sin x = +1/2. The sign was lost when moving the 1 to the other side.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error when isolating sin x

wrong.rationale: Places the reference angle π/6 in Quadrants II and III, where cosine (not sine) is negative. sin(5π/6) = +1/2, not −1/2.
wrong.error_pattern: Applying the cosine sign rule to sine

wrong.rationale: Finds the Quadrant III solution but omits the Quadrant IV solution, 11π/6, where sine is also −1/2.
wrong.error_pattern: Omitting the second solution

change_note: Equation needs isolating sin x first; negative value.

title: Tangent equation on [0, 2π)
stem: Use the unit circle to answer this. Considering only angles from 0 up to, but not including, 2π, which choice lists every angle x that satisfies tan x + 1 = 0?

correct.rationale: tan x = −1. Tangent is negative in Quadrants II and IV, where the reference angle π/4 gives x = π − π/4 = 3π/4 and x = 2π − π/4 = 7π/4.

wrong.rationale: These are the solutions of tan x = +1. The sign was lost when isolating tan x.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error when isolating tan x

wrong.rationale: Pairs Quadrant II with Quadrant III, but tangent is positive in Quadrant III: tan(5π/4) = +1, not −1.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong quadrant pairing

wrong.rationale: Finds one solution but ignores that tangent has period π, so 3π/4 + π = 7π/4 is also a solution in the interval.
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring the period π of tangent

change_note: Tangent equation; period π means solutions are π apart.

title: Principal value of arcsine
stem: A technician records θ = sin⁻¹(−√3/2), using the principal range of the inverse sine function. What is θ?

correct.rationale: The principal range of sin⁻¹ is [−π/2, π/2], and sin(−π/3) = −√3/2 there.

wrong.rationale: sin(π/3) = +√3/2, which is positive. The sign was dropped.
wrong.error_pattern: Dropping the negative sign

wrong.rationale: sin(4π/3) = −√3/2, but 4π/3 is outside the principal range [−π/2, π/2] of inverse sine.
wrong.error_pattern: Giving an angle outside the principal range

wrong.rationale: sin(5π/3) = −√3/2, but 5π/3 is outside the principal range [−π/2, π/2] of inverse sine.
wrong.error_pattern: Giving a coterminal angle outside the principal range

change_note: Inverse sine with a negative value, whose answer is a negative angle.

title: Principal value of arctangent
stem: Evaluate tan⁻¹(−1), using the principal range of the inverse tangent function.

correct.rationale: The principal range of tan⁻¹ is (−π/2, π/2), and tan(−π/4) = −1 there.

wrong.rationale: tan(3π/4) = −1, but 3π/4 is outside the principal range (−π/2, π/2) of inverse tangent.
wrong.error_pattern: Giving an angle outside the principal range

wrong.rationale: tan(7π/4) = −1, but 7π/4 is outside the principal range (−π/2, π/2) of inverse tangent.
wrong.error_pattern: Giving a coterminal angle outside the principal range

wrong.rationale: tan(π/4) = +1, which is positive. The sign was dropped.
wrong.error_pattern: Dropping the negative sign

change_note: Inverse tangent with different principal range.

title: Principal value of arccosine, √2/2
stem: The angle θ satisfies cos θ = −√2/2 and is the output of the inverse cosine function. What is θ?

correct.rationale: The output of cos⁻¹ lies in [0, π], and cos(3π/4) = −√2/2 there.

wrong.rationale: cos(−3π/4) = −√2/2, but −3π/4 is outside the range [0, π] of inverse cosine.
wrong.error_pattern: Giving a negative angle outside the principal range

wrong.rationale: cos(5π/4) = −√2/2, but 5π/4 is outside the range [0, π] of inverse cosine.
wrong.error_pattern: Giving an angle outside the principal range

wrong.rationale: cos(π/4) = +√2/2, which is positive. The sign was dropped.
wrong.error_pattern: Dropping the negative sign

change_note: Reference angle π/4; stem phrased as an output-of-inverse condition.

title: Polar to Cartesian, (−4, π/3)
stem: A robot's sensor reports a target location in polar form with a negative radius, namely r = −4 at angle θ = π/3. Converting this reading to rectangular form, which ordered pair (x, y) gives the target's Cartesian coordinates?

wrong.rationale: Ignores the negative radius: 4·(1/2) = 2 and 4·(√3/2) = 2√3.
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring the negative radius

wrong.rationale: Applies the negative radius to x but not to y: x = −2, y = +4·(√3/2) = 2√3.
wrong.error_pattern: Applying the sign of r to only one coordinate

wrong.rationale: Interchanges the components: x = r sin θ = −4·(√3/2) = −2√3 and y = r cos θ = −4·(1/2) = −2.
wrong.error_pattern: Interchanging sine and cosine

change_note: Different r and θ (−4, π/3).

title: Polar to Cartesian, (6, 5π/6)
stem: On a radar screen, an aircraft appears at distance r = 6 from the origin along the direction θ = 5π/6. Converting from polar to rectangular form, which ordered pair (x, y) gives its position?

wrong.rationale: Uses the reference angle π/6 for both coordinates without adjusting for Quadrant II: x = 6·(√3/2) = 3√3. But cos(5π/6) is negative.
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring the quadrant sign of cosine

wrong.rationale: Interchanges the components: x = 6 sin(5π/6) = 3 and y = 6 cos(5π/6) = −3√3.
wrong.error_pattern: Interchanging sine and cosine

wrong.rationale: Gets x right but gives y a negative sign: sin(5π/6) = +1/2, so y = +3, not −3.
wrong.error_pattern: Wrong sign for sine in Quadrant II

change_note: Positive radius with a Quadrant II angle; sign of cosine is the key.

title: Polar to Cartesian, (−6, 7π/6)
stem: A point is plotted using polar coordinates (r, θ) = (−6, 7π/6). What are its Cartesian coordinates?

wrong.rationale: Ignores the negative radius: 6·(−√3/2) = −3√3 and 6·(−1/2) = −3.
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring the negative radius

wrong.rationale: Applies the negative radius to x correctly, 3√3, but forgets it for y: y = 6·(−1/2) = −3 instead of −6·(−1/2) = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Applying the sign of r to only one coordinate

wrong.rationale: Interchanges the components: x = r sin θ = −6·(−1/2) = 3 and y = r cos θ = −6·(−√3/2) = 3√3.
wrong.error_pattern: Interchanging sine and cosine

change_note: Negative radius with a Quadrant III angle, double sign interplay.

title: Polar circle r = 6cos θ
stem: Consider the graph of the polar equation r = 6cos θ drawn in the polar plane. Which of the following correctly describes the shape and location of this graph?

correct.text: A circle of radius 3 centered at (3, 0)
correct.rationale: Multiplying by r gives x² + y² = 6x, which becomes (x − 3)² + y² = 9.

wrong.text: A circle of radius 3 centered at (0, 3)
wrong.rationale: A center on the y-axis corresponds to a sine form such as r = 6sin θ. Here x² + y² = 6x gives (x − 3)² + y² = 9, centered at (3, 0).
wrong.error_pattern: Mixing up sine and cosine forms

wrong.text: A circle of radius 6 centered at the origin
wrong.rationale: That would be r = 6. For r = 6cos θ, x² + y² = 6x gives (x − 3)² + y² = 9, which is not centered at the origin.
wrong.error_pattern: Reading the coefficient as a constant radius

wrong.text: A circle of radius 6 centered at (3, 0)
wrong.rationale: Gets the center right but uses the coefficient 6 as the radius. (x − 3)² + y² = 9 gives radius 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the coefficient as the radius

change_note: Cosine form (center on the x-axis) instead of sine form.

title: Polar circle r = −10sin θ
stem: For the polar curve r = −10sin θ, which description is correct?

correct.text: A circle of radius 5 centered at (0, −5)
correct.rationale: Multiplying by r gives x² + y² = −10y, which becomes x² + (y + 5)² = 25.

wrong.text: A circle of radius 5 centered at (0, 5)
wrong.rationale: Ignores the negative sign. x² + y² = −10y gives x² + (y + 5)² = 25, centered at (0, −5), not (0, 5).
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring the negative coefficient

wrong.text: A circle of radius 5 centered at (−5, 0)
wrong.rationale: A center on the x-axis corresponds to a cosine form. Here x² + (y + 5)² = 25 is centered at (0, −5).
wrong.error_pattern: Mixing up sine and cosine forms

wrong.text: A circle of radius 10 centered at (0, −10)
wrong.rationale: Uses the coefficient 10 as the radius and for the center distance. x² + (y + 5)² = 25 gives radius 5, center (0, −5).
wrong.error_pattern: Using the coefficient as the radius

change_note: Negative coefficient with sine, so the circle is below the origin.

title: Polar circle r = −2cos θ
stem: A designer sketches the polar equation r = −2cos θ and notices that the radius is negative for many angles. Which description of the resulting curve is correct?

correct.text: A circle of radius 1 centered at (−1, 0)
correct.rationale: Multiplying by r gives x² + y² = −2x, which becomes (x + 1)² + y² = 1.

wrong.text: A circle of radius 1 centered at (1, 0)
wrong.rationale: Ignores the negative sign. x² + y² = −2x gives (x + 1)² + y² = 1, centered at (−1, 0), not (1, 0).
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring the negative coefficient

wrong.text: A circle of radius 1 centered at (0, −1)
wrong.rationale: A center on the y-axis corresponds to a sine form. Here (x + 1)² + y² = 1 is centered at (−1, 0).
wrong.error_pattern: Mixing up sine and cosine forms

wrong.text: A circle of radius 2 centered at (−1, 0)
wrong.rationale: Gets the center right but uses the coefficient 2 as the radius. (x + 1)² + y² = 1 gives radius 1.
wrong.error_pattern: Using the coefficient as the radius

change_note: Negative cosine; circle left of the origin with radius 1.

title: Zeros of a biquadratic
stem:
No calculator is permitted.

The polynomial q(x) = x⁴ − 13x² + 36 has which complete set of real zeros?

correct.rationale: Let u = x². Then u² − 13u + 36 = (u − 4)(u − 9) = 0, so x² = 4 or x² = 9, giving x = ±2 and x = ±3.

wrong.rationale: These are the values u = ±4, ±9 treated as x. The solutions of x² = 4 and x² = 9 are x = ±2 and ±3.
wrong.error_pattern: Confusing values of x² with values of x

wrong.rationale: Takes only the positive square roots of x² = 4 and x² = 9, omitting −2 and −3.
wrong.error_pattern: Omitting negative roots

wrong.rationale: Omits the positive root +3 from x² = 9.
wrong.error_pattern: Omitting one root of x² = 9

change_note: Different quartic (13, 36) and different error set.

title: Real zeros when x² = −4 appears
stem:
No calculator is permitted.

While sketching a graph, a student factors the polynomial r(x) = x⁴ + 3x² − 4 and then finds where it crosses the x-axis. Which choice is the complete set of real zeros of r?

correct.rationale: Factor as (x² + 4)(x² − 1). The factor x² + 4 has no real zeros, and x² − 1 = 0 gives x = ±1.

wrong.rationale: Treats x² = −4 as if it gave x = ±2. But x² = −4 has no real solutions (its solutions are ±2i).
wrong.error_pattern: Taking square roots of a negative number as real

wrong.rationale: Solves u² + 3u − 4 = (u + 4)(u − 1) = 0 for u = x² and reports u = −4 and u = 1 as the values of x.
wrong.error_pattern: Confusing values of x² with values of x

wrong.rationale: Omits the root −1 from x² = 1 (and discards x² = −4 correctly).
wrong.error_pattern: Omitting the negative root

change_note: Quadratic in x² has one negative root, so only some zeros are real.

title: Cubic zeros by grouping
stem:
No calculator is permitted.

The polynomial p(x) = x³ − 3x² − 4x + 12 has which complete set of real zeros?

correct.rationale: Group: x²(x − 3) − 4(x − 3) = (x − 3)(x² − 4) = (x − 3)(x − 2)(x + 2), so the zeros are 3, 2, and −2.

wrong.rationale: Omits −2 from x² − 4 = 0, which has both x = 2 and x = −2.
wrong.error_pattern: Omitting the negative root

wrong.rationale: Solves x² − 4 = 0 but ignores the factor (x − 3), which gives the zero x = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Ignoring a factor

wrong.rationale: Reads the factor (x − 3) as giving x = −3 instead of x = 3.
wrong.error_pattern: Sign error when reading a zero from a factor

change_note: Cubic factored by grouping instead of a quartic in x².
